title: Reliable actuarial measurement of unprecedented catastrophe losses

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a dependable way to estimate the range and likelihood of catastrophe losses when past experience contains few comparable events and future conditions are changing. It would combine evidence about physical hazards, the people and property exposed, their vulnerability to damage, and insurance losses to produce loss distributions that remain useful across specified hazards, regions and changing conditions. Reliability would include identifying which assumptions drive an estimate and recognizing when the evidence cannot justify useful bounds.

Existing catastrophe models already combine physical, engineering and loss evidence. The proposed advance therefore lies in independently demonstrated transfer to materially different conditions, together with tested uncertainty estimates and explicit limits on extrapolation. AIR's May 2021 model submission, as described in the supplied review, documents damage relationships informed by engineering studies, damage surveys and available loss data; combining these ingredients alone would not constitute the breakthrough.

significance.text: If achieved, independently tested catastrophe-loss distributions would give insurers, reinsurers and public risk pools a stronger basis for pricing, reserves, reinsurance purchases and capital decisions where their own loss histories provide little guidance. Catastrophe models already inform technical pricing of reinsurance contracts and insurance-linked securities. The potential advance is a more dependable basis for those decisions when conditions differ materially from the historical record.

A particularly consequential capability would be recognizing when extrapolation is defensible and when a seemingly precise loss estimate rests on weak assumptions. The reviewed hurricane study illustrates why this matters: incorporating projected changes in overall storm frequency reverses the direction of its median loss changes. Better measurement could make such dependencies visible before financial commitments are made, although it would not eliminate the underlying uncertainty.

More informative loss estimates could also support emergency management, hazard mitigation, public disaster financing and risk pooling. The supplied Verisk whitepaper describes these applications and discusses affordability constraints, but it is a vendor account of model uses rather than independent evidence that better measurement produces these outcomes.

Conditional impact synthesis: broader insurance availability and safer development are possible downstream benefits, but they would also require sufficient capital, affordable prices and effective public decisions. Accurate measurement does not itself finance losses, prevent damage or make every risk insurable. The revolutionary potential concerns improved decisions under specified changing conditions; no supplied benchmark establishes a ranking against other innovations.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is transferable loss estimation with independently tested uncertainty across specified catastrophe hazards, regions and changing conditions. Rare extreme losses provide limited observational evidence, while changes in hazards, exposure and vulnerability complicate comparisons over time. Dependence also matters: the reviewed study describes hurricane events in which larger wind losses accompany larger flood losses, so treating damage contributions as independent can misrepresent combined losses.

Concrete barriers include establishing physically justified links from changing hazards to damage, representing dependent loss contributions, and estimating extreme tails beyond the observed record. In the reviewed hurricane work, tail estimation extends a 72-year historical record using a commercial stochastic hurricane catalog. Its supplement also assumes that a projected proportional increase in precipitation produces an equal proportional increase in flood depth. These choices expose dependencies that require separate testing; their inclusion does not establish that the resulting tails are calibrated.

Scientific synthesis: a transferable framework would need to distinguish uncertainty supported by observations from uncertainty introduced through assumptions and simulation, and detect when new conditions exceed its demonstrated scope. Useful predictive guarantees require restrictions on possible future regimes; arbitrary unknown changes cannot support nontrivial distribution-free guarantees. This is a logical boundary on the objective, not a theorem established by the supplied hurricane paper. The supplied evidence establishes neither achievement of the proposed capability nor its absence across the entire field.

current_state.text: On 4 November 2024, Francesco Comola, Bernhard Märtl, Hilary Paul, Christian Bruns and Klaus Sapelza published a study combining North Atlantic hurricane evidence, US insurance-loss information and stochastic modeling to estimate losses under +2°C and +4°C warming scenarios. It uses NOAA's HURDAT2 hurricane dataset and more than 70 years of historical evidence. These are conditional modeled estimates, rather than observations of losses in those future warming conditions.

The study addresses US losses from North Atlantic hurricanes, including dependent contributions from wind, precipitation and storm surge. Modeling several damage mechanisms within hurricanes is relevant progress, but it does not demonstrate transfer across distinct catastrophe perils and regions. Nor does agreement with, or use of, a commercial hurricane catalog independently establish calibration of rare-loss probabilities.

The main analysis holds overall storm frequency unchanged. Supplementary analysis incorporating projected frequency changes instead produces decreasing median losses, reversing the direction found under the main assumption. This difference reflects alternative assumptions rather than an established contradiction. Other consequential dependencies include commercial stochastic-catalog augmentation beyond the 72-year historical record and the assumed proportional relationship between precipitation increases and flood-depth increases.

Earlier commercial documentation establishes that substantial evidence integration already exists. The reviewed portion of AIR's May 2021 submission describes engineering- and loss-informed damage relationships, while Verisk's 2023 whitepaper describes insurance and public-sector applications. These documents support the existence and use of relevant modeling components, but do not establish the proposed framework's independent validation across changing conditions. The AIR extraction truncates on page 38 and cannot establish the submission's full validation record; the Verisk account is vendor-authored.

According to the supplied review, complete main-article HTML and the complete eight-page technical supplement were available in saved copies. The main PDF had extraction warnings, but usable HTML supported the assessment of the methods. Figure images and supplementary plotted curves were not visually inspected, so the conclusions here rely on the reviewed text rather than independent examination of those graphics.

Evidence-scope synthesis: the supplied material documents relevant methods and important limitations, but does not establish feasibility of the full proposed framework. It also cannot establish whether that capability remained absent across the field as of 1 November 2026, because no bounded search entries were supplied. This limitation does not invalidate the dated 2024 results or show that the wider objective is impossible.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: register models, assumptions and uncertainty ranges before evaluation across several specified hazards and regions, including conditions withheld from development. Use independent datasets and subsequently observed events to assess whether predicted loss distributions are calibrated, uncertainty ranges achieve credible coverage, and warnings identify conditions in which assumptions fail. Define calibration metrics, coverage targets, dependence handling and decision-relevant usefulness before evaluation; these are proposed requirements, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Preregistered loss distributions demonstrate calibration and coverage across withheld conditions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed rare-tail assessment: evaluate extreme-loss claims with independent physical evidence and justified simulations, while keeping their conditional contribution distinct from observed-event validation. A few years of outcomes cannot by themselves establish a claimed 1-in-200 annual exceedance probability. The reviewed study's need to augment a 72-year record illustrates the observational constraint; simulation can extend assessment beyond that record, but does not supply independently observed centuries or guarantee correct tail probabilities.
completion_criteria.label: Extreme-loss claims assessed through independent physical evidence and justified simulations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed robustness assessment: independently test influential physical relationships and compare results under plausible alternative assumptions, including event frequency, dependence among damage mechanisms and hazard-to-damage mappings. The hurricane study's frequency sensitivity and precipitation-to-flood-depth assumption provide concrete examples of assumptions that such an assessment should expose and investigate.
completion_criteria.label: Independent robustness tests expose sensitivity to plausible alternative assumptions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundary: independent teams should be able to reproduce material estimates and sensitivity findings using sufficiently documented data, code and model assumptions, with any access restrictions made explicit. Convincing performance would include useful estimates within declared operating conditions and clear indications when evidence is inadequate. Successful finite tests would demonstrate breadth over the tested conditions; they would not establish literal universality or reliability under arbitrary future changes.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce material estimates and sensitivities within declared limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — ACT-02, “Trustworthy, near-instant insurance settlement at negligible per-claim cost,” concerns resolving individual claims after losses occur. ACT-01 concerns estimating distributions of possible catastrophe losses. Settlement records could inform loss measurement, but fast, trustworthy claims handling and reliable prediction are distinct capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis — ACT-03, “A scalable actuarial architecture for financing correlated catastrophes,” has the closest conceptual overlap. ACT-01 would estimate loss magnitude, uncertainty and dependence; ACT-03 would address financing correlated losses. Measurement could inform financing decisions, while adequate financing would still require its own architecture and resources. Only ACT-03's title was supplied, so this distinction is conceptual rather than a verified comparison of detailed specifications.

Roster-based synthesis — ACT-04, “Reliable long-horizon mortality and longevity forecasting with honest uncertainty,” shares the challenge of making projections under changing conditions while reporting uncertainty honestly. Its subject is mortality and longevity rather than catastrophe damage and insured losses; success in either domain would not establish transfer to the other.

Roster-based synthesis — ACT-05, “Dependable long-horizon economic scenarios for actuarial liabilities,” concerns economic conditions affecting liabilities. Such scenarios could provide financial context for catastrophe exposure and loss valuation, but reliable economic scenarios would not by themselves validate physical hazard, vulnerability or catastrophe-tail estimates.

Roster-based synthesis — ACT-06, “Reliable long-term actuarial projection of healthcare costs under structural change,” shares the problem of extrapolating when underlying drivers change. Its focus on healthcare costs requires different evidence and mechanisms from catastrophe-loss measurement, even where approaches to uncertainty and changing assumptions overlap.

Roster-based synthesis — ACT-07, “Accessible lifetime retirement income through transparent, resilient risk pooling,” concerns delivering retirement income through pooling. ACT-01 could contribute methods for assessing uncertainty and dependence, but retirement-income design and catastrophe-loss estimation remain separate objectives. Beyond their supplied titles, detailed specifications for ACT-02 and ACT-04 through ACT-07 were unavailable.

unresolved_issues: Whether independently validated transfer at the proposed scope has been achieved elsewhere, or remains an open capability as of 1 November 2026, cannot be determined from the supplied evidence and empty bounded search record.
The hazards, regions, changing conditions and practical operating boundaries for a convincing demonstration remain unspecified.
Calibration metrics, uncertainty-coverage targets, dependence handling and thresholds for decision-relevant usefulness require definition before evaluation.
Independent validation of rare tails, the precipitation-to-flood-depth relationship and transfer beyond the reviewed US hurricane setting remains unestablished by these materials.
The truncated AIR extraction does not establish its full validation record; vendor descriptions of model applications do not independently establish predictive reliability.
Detailed relationships with the other roster concepts remain provisional because only their IDs and titles were supplied.

brief.title: Reliable estimates of unfamiliar disaster losses
possible: Insurers and public disaster funds could estimate how much disasters might cost, and how likely different losses are, even when past events offer little guidance. Those estimates would remain dependable across tested hazards, places and changing conditions.
They could also tell when an estimate rests on weak assumptions and when there is too little evidence to give a useful range.
why: Insurers could set prices, hold reserves and buy insurance for their own losses on a stronger basis. Public disaster funds could better plan how much money they need when conditions differ from the past.

Making the assumptions visible would help decision-makers understand what could change their financial commitments. Better loss estimates could also support emergency planning and spending to reduce damage.

sources.showed: They modeled US hurricane losses under warming, combining storm and insurance data. Losses rose when storm frequency stayed unchanged; allowing projected frequency changes reversed the direction of median losses.
sources.quote: The contribution to the AAL from precipitation-driven losses may show an even larger percentage increase than those from wind and storm surge losses.
sources.cited_for: The study estimates average annual loss, or AAL, and shows how assumptions can change projected hurricane costs.
sources.not_established: It does not establish dependable loss probabilities across different disaster types, regions and changing conditions.

sources.showed: They combined residential flood-loss data across countries and tested predictions on other floods. Performance varied between river floods and floods caused by heavy rain.
sources.quote: Predictions for the German and Italian fluvial floods were better than for pluvial floods or the 1993 Meuse river flood.
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates tests of whether flood-loss estimates remain useful beyond the events used to build a model.
sources.not_established: It does not establish reliable uncertainty ranges across unfamiliar disasters and changing conditions.

sources.showed: They applied sensitivity analysis, which tests how changing assumptions affects results, to a commercial flood-loss model in the Rhine basin and Queensland.
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates ways to identify assumptions that drive uncertainty in large flood-loss models.
sources.not_established: Finding influential assumptions does not establish that predicted losses or their probabilities are correct.

shown: Researchers have tested flood-loss models across countries and flood types. Paprotny and colleagues reproduced average losses in a French coastal flood better than the alternative models they compared, though performance varied across events.

Comola and colleagues modeled how warming could change US hurricane losses. Their results show why assumptions matter: including projected changes in storm frequency reversed the direction of median loss changes.
missing: Independent demonstrations that predicted loss ranges remain reliable across specified disasters, regions and changing conditions are still needed.
Claims about the rarest, largest losses need independent physical support and justified simulations beyond short historical records.
Links from hazards to damage, including how wind and flood losses rise together, need separate testing.
Independent teams still need to reproduce material estimates and identify when conditions exceed the models’ tested limits.

milestones.label: Advance predictions hold up across unfamiliar conditions
milestones.explanation: Models, assumptions and test targets would be registered in advance, then independent data and later events would test probabilities, ranges and failure warnings across hazards and regions. This would establish where predictions hold up.

milestones.label: Extreme losses withstand independent physical checks
milestones.explanation: Extreme-loss claims would face independent physical evidence and justified simulations, assessed separately from observed events. This would test claims that short histories cannot settle.

milestones.label: Independent tests reveal which assumptions change the answer
milestones.explanation: Independent tests would vary storm frequency, links between damage types and relationships between hazards and damage. This would reveal which plausible assumptions materially change estimated losses.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results within stated limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would reproduce key estimates and their responses to changed assumptions using documented data, code and assumptions. Useful results and clear warnings would establish the conditions in which estimates can be trusted.

uncertain: Which hazards, regions and changing conditions would count as a convincing demonstration?
How accurate must predicted probabilities and uncertainty ranges be to support practical decisions?
How far can tests support estimates of unprecedented losses when future conditions differ from everything observed?

page.title: Catastrophe loss modeling under nonstationarity
page.definition: Catastrophe models predict loss probabilities and uncertainty after specified changes in climate, exposure (assets at risk) or vulnerability (susceptibility to damage). Independent tests on observed losses establish the conditions under which these predictions remain valid.

goal.need: Swiss Re estimated worldwide natural-catastrophe economic losses in 2025 at USD 220 billion, including USD 107 billion insured, in 2025 prices. NOAA and NSF identified combining climate projections with catastrophe modeling as an insurance-sector research objective.

figures.note: Swiss Re estimates; insured losses form part of economic losses.

completion.title: Independent validation supports catastrophe loss probabilities and uncertainty after a specified regime change.
completion.criterion: An independent validation, published after peer review, finds a catastrophe model's loss probabilities and uncertainty intervals adequate against observed losses from a specified peril–region regime whose changed climate, exposure or vulnerability conditions were excluded from model development. It identifies the conditions outside which extrapolation is unsupported. The acceptance tests and tolerances belong to that published validation; the cited standards supply no common numerical cut-off.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; proposed synthesis of actuarial and insurance-supervisory validation requirements.
completion.basis: Searched ASOP Nos. 38 and 56, IAIS catastrophe-model safeguards and climate-risk guidance, and Florida's 2025 hurricane and flood standards for a test of regime transfer with calibrated uncertainty; none supplies this combined threshold. Their requirements concern validation for a specified purpose. The proposed test restricts the claim to an observed change and independent evaluation.

milestones.title: A catastrophe model's loss estimates reasonably reproduce historical observations.
milestones.criterion: Output reasonably represents modeled losses when compared with historical observations; ASOP No. 38 sets no universal error tolerance. Published online on 2 December 2020, Paprotny et al.'s flood model estimated EUR 163 million against EUR 408 million in claims for two French departments after Xynthia on 28 February 2010. The paper attributes much of the discrepancy to missing affected buildings.
milestones.set_by: Actuarial Standards Board, ASOP No. 38, section 3.5; a qualitative validation criterion applied according to intended purpose.
milestones.threshold_quote: the output reasonably represents that which is being modeled.

milestones.title: A catastrophe model's loss responses to varied inputs are judged reasonable for its intended use.
milestones.criterion: Changes in modeled losses under varied inputs are reasonable for the intended use; ASOP No. 38 sets no numerical sensitivity limit. On 4 November 2024, Comola et al. reported that adding projected storm-frequency changes reversed median US hurricane-loss changes under +2°C and +4°C scenarios. On 15 April 2026, Pianosi et al. reported 400 Rhine-basin runs varying four inputs; halving vulnerability-curve uncertainty made event-set uncertainty dominant in as many spatial units.
milestones.set_by: Actuarial Standards Board, ASOP No. 38, section 3.5, item 4; a qualitative sensitivity criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: evaluating the reasonableness of changes in the output due to variations in the user input.

milestones.title: A catastrophe model retains reasonably consistent outputs on withheld data.
milestones.criterion: Output on data withheld during model development remains reasonably consistent with output developed without those data; ASOP No. 56 supplies no numerical tolerance. Paprotny et al. used fivefold cross-validation across data from 11 flood events: nominal 95% uncertainty ranges included observed building-loss totals in 5 events and contents-loss totals in 7. Fivefold validation does not itself establish transfer to an unseen climate regime.
milestones.set_by: Actuarial Standards Board, ASOP No. 56, sections 2.4 and 3.6.2(b); hold-out validation is a recognized method selected according to intended purpose.
milestones.threshold_quote: evaluating whether the model applied to hold‐out data produces model output that is reasonably consistent with model output developed without the hold‐out data

milestones.title: Independent validation confirms a catastrophe model is adequate for its specified purpose.
milestones.criterion: Independent validation confirms that the catastrophe model and supporting processes are adequate for their specified purpose, including quantitative and qualitative assessment of the whole model and its components. Validators have appropriate independence, skills and experience; independence may be internal or external to the insurer. This establishes adequacy within the declared application before evaluation extends to a changed regime.
milestones.set_by: International Association of Insurance Supervisors, Insurance Capital Standard, section 5.2.4.7, Safeguard 2 and explanatory paragraphs 39–41; written for internationally active insurance groups.
milestones.threshold_quote: confirm that the natural catastrophe model and the supporting processes are adequate and appropriate for the purpose.

not_found: No independent validation of both loss probabilities and uncertainty intervals after a specified regime change was identified in the three supplied studies.
The supplied studies establish no case-specific results for earthquake, wildfire or severe convective storm models.
The Nature HTML for the hurricane study was inaccessible; its published PDF was available from the German National Library.

results.finding: For 100 simulated event sets, median US hurricane average annual loss rose 10% under +2°C warming.
results.detail: The authors assessed responses to projected climate inputs. Including projected storm-frequency changes reversed the direction of median loss changes; confidence in those frequency projections was low.
results.quote:
The median changes in hurricane climatology may cause the average annual loss (AAL) to increase from USD 21.8 billion in the historical baseline to USD 23.9 billion (+10%) and USD 25.3 billion (+15%) in the  +2 °C and  +4 °C scenarios, respectively (Fig.
4
a).

results.finding: For 739 observations in the 2014 Italian flood, modeled total building loss differed from observations by 3%.
results.detail: This event-level result does not imply comparable accuracy for every flood or household.

results.finding: Across 11 flood events, using alternative JRC exposure estimates greatly increased total contents-loss prediction error.
results.detail: The study assesses the effect of changing exposure inputs, but does not establish that the resulting loss responses are reasonable for a specified intended use.
results.quote:
Using JRC expo-
sure estimates vastly increases error in predicting total contents loss, but has limited
effect on building loss predictions.

results.finding: In fivefold validation across 11 flood events, 95% uncertainty ranges covered observed building-loss totals in 5 events.
results.detail: The ranges covered contents-loss totals in 7 of 11 events. Coverage was limited, and the paper does not establish transfer to an unseen climate regime.
results.quote:
Also, the 95% uncertainty ranges of the modelled estimates of 
building loss cover observed totals for only 5 out of 11 events, while for contents, it is 7 
out of 11 (Fig. 6 ).

results.finding: In 400 Rhine-basin model runs, halving vulnerability-curve uncertainty made event-set uncertainty dominant in as many spatial units.
results.detail: The authors judged the sensitivity analysis tolerably robust to the assumed damage-ratio ranges. Results depend on the inputs and ranges selected; flood-defence uncertainty was excluded.
results.quote:
the uncertainties in the vulnerability
curves (i.e. the variability ranges of the damage ratios) need

event set, to become dominant in as many spatial units.

results.finding: For 106 historical U.S. hurricanes, the model’s loss estimates had an RMSE of USD 7.0 billion.
results.detail: The weighted-rank model was optimized on the historical sample, and predicted loss ranks were assigned observed losses. Some events remained poorly predicted.
results.quote: Across our sample of 106 historical hurricanes, this prediction model has the lowest RMSE (USD 7.0 billion) when hazard, exposure and vulnerability predictors are ranked and summed, while also applying optimal weights (Fig. 8c).

results.finding: INSYDE 2.0 estimated median flood damage of €7.53 million for 294 buildings in Caldogno.
results.detail: Observed damage was €8.35 million in 2021 euros. The estimate uses probabilistic sampling to fill missing inputs; the model tended to overestimate smaller losses.

results.finding: Swiss hail model: all 33 largest observed hail days from 2002–2021 had building losses estimated within one order of magnitude.
results.detail: The 33 events accounted for 91% of observed hail damages. The model was calibrated on historical claims; five-fold cross-validation found similar skill on independent verification data. Radar-based hail detection remained a major source of uncertainty.
results.quote: Focusing on observed extreme hail days from 2013–2021 (2002–2021), the largest 17 (33) events which make up 92 % (91 %) of all hail damages are modelled with the correct OOM.

results.finding: Severe convective storm residential damage model: large claims sample, size unspecified; predicted aggregate damage deviated less than 2% from observations.
results.detail: The model was assessed using diagnostics and cross-validation on object-level insurance claims and meteorological observations.
results.quote: Multiple model diagnostics and a cross-validation procedure show that the compound vulnerability function predicts aggregated damage with high accuracy, deviating less than 2% from the observed aggregate damage.

results.finding: For US severe convective storms, a 10,000-year event set showed a 60% increase in estimated 100-year loss with tornado intensity clustering.
results.detail: Using US residential exposure, PartnerRe judged the model fit for property portfolio risk assessment. Modeled clustering more closely matched observed severe tornado clustering when intensity clustering was included.

results.finding: For 431 German flood-loss observations, the multivariable beta model’s 90% prediction intervals covered 95% of cross-validated observations.
results.detail: Tenfold cross-validation assesses coverage on withheld observations, but the reported result does not compare those outputs with model outputs developed using the withheld data.

results.finding: An earthquake property-damage model was tested on 4 out-of-sample events; its estimates were generally near published estimates.
results.detail: The model was trained on 40 earlier earthquakes. For the Virginia test case, its estimates exceeded all cited literature estimates. The paper does not directly compare withheld-data performance with development-data performance.
results.quote:

results.finding: Hailstorm loss model: prediction-interval coverage was near the intended levels across 130 withheld storms.
results.detail: The censored factor-copula model showed better holdout calibration than the two-part model. Coverage is reported graphically without exact values; the test does not establish transfer to a new climate regime.
results.quote: The dependence models appear to obtain the desired coverage probabilities near the 45-degree line, compared to the lower coverage probabilities of the independence models.

results.finding: One Moody’s hurricane model was independently reviewed; its replication of known hurricane losses was verified against standard S-5.
